docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This page serves as an evidence portfolio of the work completed throughout the semester in the Embedded Systems course, taught by Professor Oliver Ochoa Garcia.

docs.title: Course Objective
docs.text:
Learn to design and program embedded systems at the hardware level using the RP2350, integrating sensors, actuators, communication, and real-time processing to develop autonomous and functional systems.

Within this course, fundamental topics for the development and programming of embedded systems are covered, including:

  • Development Environment Setup — Installation and use of the Pico SDK, CMake, GDB, and OpenOCD, as well as ESD safety practices.
  • Low-Level Programming — Register-level programming, GPIO, bitwise operations, finite state machines (FSMs), timers, and interrupts.
  • Serial Communication — Implementation of UART, ring buffers, command-line interfaces (CLI), and debugging techniques.
  • Sensor and Actuator Interfacing — Use of PWM to control LEDs, servomotors, and DC motors, as well as ADC for analog signal acquisition and processing.
  • Signal Processing and Generation — Implementation of PIO (Programmable I/O) and DMA to efficiently generate, capture, and transfer signals.
  • Performance and Reliability — Analysis of performance, latency, and jitter; use of watchdogs, low-power techniques, EMC, memory architecture, and multicore programming.
  • Testing and Validation — Application of unit testing and debugging techniques to verify proper system operation.
  • Capstone Project: Micromouse — Integration of the acquired knowledge to develop an autonomous system capable of navigating a competitive environment.

docs.title: Block 1 - GPIO
docs.text: Goal: to understand and control GPIO peripherals through memory-mapped registers, bitwise operations, masks, and RP2350 SIO registers.

docs.title: What I Learned
docs.text: In this practice, I learned how to control the GPIO pins of the RP2W and how each register affects their behavior. I also learned how binary numbers and masks can be used to control specific pins, and how the << operation moves bits to create the value needed. Finally, I understood better how the Pico SDK functions work and how they are connected to the SIO registers.

docs.title: Exercise 1 — 4 bit binary counter
docs.text:
Use the four LEDs as a 4-bit binary number.

The program must count: 1 → 2 → 3 → ... → 15 → 0

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
At the beginning, Gio and I were a little confused about the theory behind the exercise, so we asked ChatGPT for an example code to help us understand it. The code worked, but it was quite different from what our teacher later explained in class. After going over the concepts again, especially binary numbers and masks, we were able to write our own code.

Code gived by Chatgpt: 

  while (true) {
        // Apagar todos los LEDs
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
        // Encender los LEDs según el número binario
        sio_hw->gpio_set = number;
        // Esperar
        sleep_ms(500);
        // Siguiente número
        number++;
        // Regresar a 0 después de 15
        if (number > 15) {
            number = 0;
        }

Code made by ourselfs: 

sio_hw->gpio_set = (counter);
sleep_ms(200);
sio_hw->gpio_clr = (0b1111<<0);
sleep_ms(200);
counter++;

docs.title: Exercise 2 — Bouncing light
docs.text: Create a light that moves across the four LEDs and then returns.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
For this exercise, we went over the theory again and understood better how to move the bits between the four LEDs. With this, we were able to create the code ourselves.

Code: 

   while (true) 
   {for(pos=0;pos<=3;pos++)
    {  sio_hw->gpio_set = (1u<<pos);
       sleep_ms(200);
       sio_hw->gpio_clr = (1u<<pos);
       sleep_ms(200);
    }
    for(pos=3;pos>=0;pos--)
    {  sio_hw->gpio_set = (1u<<pos);
       sleep_ms(200);
       sio_hw->gpio_clr = (1u<<pos);
       sleep_ms(200);
    }
    }

docs.title: Exercise 3 — Fill and empty animation
docs.text: Create an animation that progressively fills all four LEDs and then progressively empties them.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
For this exercise, we reviewed the theory again and understood how the masks could be used to control each LED. Instead of using a counter like in the previous exercises, we decided to turn each LED on and off individually using binary values. This made the sequence easier for us to understand and follow.

Code: 

sio_hw->gpio_set = 0b0001;
sleep_ms(200);
sio_hw->gpio_set = 0b0010;
sleep_ms(200);
sio_hw->gpio_set = 0b0100;
sleep_ms(200);
sio_hw->gpio_set = 0b1000;
sleep_ms(200);

sio_hw->gpio_clr = 0b1000;
sleep_ms(200);
sio_hw->gpio_clr = 0b0100;
sleep_ms(200);
sio_hw->gpio_clr = 0b0010;
sleep_ms(200);
sio_hw->gpio_clr = 0b0001;
sleep_ms(200);

docs.title: Exercise 4 — Fill from the outside inward
docs.text: Create an animation that progressively fills all four LEDs and then progressively empties them.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
For this exercise, we used what we had learned about binary masks to control more than one LED at the same time. We first turned on the two LEDs on the outside using 1001, and then the two LEDs in the middle using 0110. After that, we turned them off in the same order.

Code: 

   while (true) {
   sio_hw->gpio_set = 0b1001;  
    sleep_ms(200);
    sio_hw->gpio_set = 0b0110;  
    sleep_ms(200);

    sio_hw->gpio_clr = 0b1001;  
    sleep_ms(200);
    sio_hw->gpio_clr = 0b0110;   
    sleep_ms(200); }

docs.title: What could have gone better
docs.text: Even though all of our codes worked correctly, I think we could have paid more attention to the theory from the beginning. We also could have experimented more with the circuit and the program to better understand how everything works. This would have helped us feel more confident with the code instead of mainly focusing on getting the expected result.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Overall, this practice helped us understand better how the GPIO pins and LEDs can be controlled using binary values and masks. At first, we were a little confused about the theory, but after reviewing it and practicing with different codes, we were able to create the four animations successfully. It also helped us see how small changes in the code can create different patterns and made us more comfortable working with the RP2350.

docs.title: 📚 Ejemplo de Documentación del Proyecto
docs.text: Plantilla genérica para documentar proyectos académicos o de ingeniería. Copia y adapta las secciones según tu necesidad.

docs.title: 1) Resumen
docs.text:
• Nombre del proyecto: Mi Proyecto
  • Equipo / Autor(es): Nombre(s)
  • Curso / Asignatura: Nombre del curso
  • Fecha: DD/MM/AAAA
  • Descripción breve: Una o dos líneas que expliquen qué hace y por qué.

Consejo

Mantén este resumen corto (máx. 5 líneas). Lo demás va en secciones específicas.

docs.title: 2) Objetivos
docs.text:
• General: Qué se pretende lograr en términos amplios.
  • Específicos:
  • OE1…
  • OE2…
  • OE3…

docs.title: 3) Alcance y Exclusiones
docs.text:
• Incluye: Qué funcionalidades/entregables sí están en el proyecto.
  • No incluye: Qué queda fuera para evitar malentendidos.

docs.title: 4) Requisitos
docs.text:
Software - SO compatible (Windows/Linux/macOS) - Python 3.x / Node 18+ / Arduino IDE / etc. - Dependencias (p. ej., pip/requirements, npm packages)

Hardware (si aplica) - MCU / Sensores / Actuadores / Fuente de poder - Herramientas (multímetro, cautín, etc.)

Conocimientos previos - Programación básica en X - Electrónica básica - Git/GitHub

docs.title: 5) Instalación
docs.text:
# 1) Clonar
git clone https://github.com/<usuario>/<repo>.git
cd <repo>

# 2) (Opcional) Crear entorno virtual
python -m venv .venv
# macOS/Linux
source .venv/bin/activate
# Windows (PowerShell)
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# 3) Instalar dependencias (ejemplos)
pip install -r requirements.txt
# o, si es Node:
npm install

docs.title: 🚀 Comandos básicos de Git (primeros pasos)
docs.text: En este curso solo usaremos los comandos esenciales de Git para trabajar con repositorios.

docs.title: 1. Clonar un repositorio
docs.text:
Copia un proyecto de GitHub a tu computadora.

git clone https://github.com/usuario/repositorio.git

docs.title: 2. Verificar cambios
docs.text:
Muestra qué archivos has modificado o agregado.

git status

docs.title: 3. Preparar cambios
docs.text:
Agrega archivos para guardarlos en el próximo commit.

git add archivo.txt
git add .   # agrega todos los archivos modificados

docs.title: 4. Guardar cambios (commit)
docs.text:
Guarda tus cambios con un mensaje descriptivo.

git commit -m "Descripción breve de los cambios"

docs.title: 5. Subir cambios al repositorio (push)
docs.text:
Envía tus commits locales al repositorio en GitHub.

git push origin main

docs.title: 6. Traer cambios del remoto (pull)
docs.text:
Actualiza tu proyecto con los últimos cambios de GitHub.

git pull origin main

docs.title: Flujo típico de trabajo
docs.text:
1. Traer cambios del remoto 

    git pull origin main

  2. Editar tus archivos de proyecto.

  3. Preparar los cambios 

    git add .

  4. Guardar los cambios 

    git commit -m "Mensaje descriptivo"

  5. Enviar los cambios al remoto 

    git push origin main

Consejo

Piensa en este ciclo como un loop infinito: cada vez que quieras contribuir → primero pull, después add + commit, y finalmente push.
